Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: A friend sends a text message complaining about having a long, boring day.
Expectation2: Arrive at the polling station during designated voting hours
Situation2: Late-afternoon errands leave just a couple of hours before the polls close.
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was about to head out the door. It was Jamie, texting, “Rough day. Can you talk?” I could almost hear the exhaustion in her words. As her friend, I knew she needed me to listen, to be there for her, especially since she rarely reached out like this. But I glanced at the clock—only two hours left before the polls closed, and I still had to pick up groceries and get to the polling station. Voting was important to me; I’d promised myself I wouldn’t miss it this year. My mind raced. If I called Jamie now, I might not make it to vote in time. If I ignored her, I’d be letting her down when she needed support. The weight of both responsibilities pressed on me, each demanding my presence, each feeling urgent in its own way. I stood frozen in my hallway, phone in hand, torn between being the friend Jamie needed and the citizen I wanted to be.
